verses.text: Then Samuel took the vial of oil, and poured it on his head, and kissed him, and said, “Hasn’t Yahweh anointed you to be prince over his inheritance?

When you have departed from me today, then you will find two men by Rachel’s tomb, on the border of Benjamin at Zelzah. They will tell you, ‘The donkeys which you went to look for have been found; and behold, your father has stopped caring about the donkeys, and is anxious for you, saying, “What shall I do for my son?”’

“Then you will go on forward from there, and you will come to the oak of Tabor. Three men will meet you there going up to God to Bethel, one carrying three young goats, and another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a bottle of wine.
They will greet you, and give you two loaves of bread, which you shall receive from their hand.

“After that you will come to the hill of God, where the garrison of the Philistines is; and it will happen, when you have come there to the city, that you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place with a lute, a tambourine, a pipe, and a harp before them; and they will be prophesying.
Then Yahweh’s Spirit will come mightily on you, and you will prophesy with them, and will be turned into another man.
Let it be, when these signs have come to you, that you do what is appropriate for the occasion; for God is with you.

“Go down ahead of me to Gilgal; and behold, I will come down to you, to offer burnt offerings, and to sacrifice sacrifices of peace offerings. Wait seven days, until I come to you, and show you what you are to do.”
It was so, that when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart; and all those signs happened that day.
When they came there to the hill, behold, a band of prophets met him; and the Spirit of God came mightily on him, and he prophesied among them.
When all who knew him before saw that, behold, he prophesied with the prophets, then the people said to one another, “What is this that has come to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
One of the same place answered, “Who is their father?” Therefore it became a proverb, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
When he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place.
Saul’s uncle said to him and to his servant, “Where did you go?” He said, “To seek the donkeys. When we saw that they were not found, we came to Samuel.”
Saul’s uncle said, “Please tell me what Samuel said to you.”
Saul said to his uncle, “He told us plainly that the donkeys were found.” But concerning the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel spoke, he didn’t tell him.
Samuel called the people together to Yahweh to Mizpah;

and he said to the children of Israel, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, says ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’

But you have today rejected your God, who himself saves you out of all your calamities and your distresses; and you have said to him, ‘No! Set a king over us.’ Now therefore present yourselves before Yahweh by your tribes, and by your thousands.”
So Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was chosen.
He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by their families; and the family of the Matrites was chosen. Then Saul the son of Kish was chosen; but when they looked for him, he could not be found.
Therefore they asked of Yahweh further, “Is there yet a man to come here?” Yahweh answered, “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.”
They ran and got him there. When he stood among the people, he was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward.
Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see him whom Yahweh has chosen, that there is no one like him among all the people?” All the people shouted, and said, “Long live the king!”
Then Samuel told the people the regulations of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before Yahweh. Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house.
Saul also went to his house to Gibeah; and the army went with him, whose hearts God had touched.
But certain worthless fellows said, “How could this man save us?” They despised him, and brought him no present. But he held his peace.

footnotes.content: That oil on Saul's head is not about anointing a hero—it's God's choice made visible. Samuel kisses him like a father would, sealing what Yahweh has already decided. When the Lord appoints, He doesn't whisper or hint; He makes it clear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rachel's tomb, Zelzah—specific places matter because Saul's story is rooted in real ground. The lost donkeys that brought him here are now found; something far greater awaits him too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The oak of Tabor, the high place, the pilgrims bearing gifts—these aren't random signs but bread for the road ahead. God meets Saul through ordinary people and familiar places, showing He doesn't need fanfare to work His will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two loaves of bread offered and received—such a small thing. Yet it echoes care and provision. The Lord often works through strangers who offer what they have, unknowingly serving His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A band of prophets making music—lute, tambourine, pipe, harp—coming down from the high place. This is not ecstasy alone; it's the sound of those who have drawn near to God in prayer and worship. Saul is about to join that company.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit comes mightily, and Saul becomes another man. Not a new self he has earned, but one the Lord gives him. In that moment, his heart is turned; what he does with it is still his choice to make.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God is with you—that is enough. When Saul hears it, he's given all he needs: assurance that he doesn't walk alone, and freedom to act as the moment requires. Wisdom is knowing both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gilgal lies ahead, seven days of waiting, then Samuel comes to show what must be done. The Lord works in seasons—times of solitude and times of clear instruction. Both are necessary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Saul turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart. The signs followed—not before—because the heart must change first. All of it happened that very day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The band of prophets met him just as Samuel said; the Spirit fell on him just as promised. Every sign has come to pass. Saul stands at the edge of his kingship, though he does not yet know what it will cost him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people's astonishment—Is Saul also among the prophets?—becomes a proverb. Sometimes what marks a man is so unexpected that onlookers cannot quite believe it. God has a way of turning the unlikely into the unforgettable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The question lingers: Who is their father? It becomes a saying passed from mouth to mouth. What seemed strange at first—a farmer's son moving in the Spirit's power—stays with the people as a memory of wonder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Saul stopped prophesying, he climbed to the high place. The sacred moment released him, and he returned to ordinary ground. Both praise and the simple act of walking away have their place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His uncle asks, Where did you go? Saul speaks plainly about the donkeys—honesty in small things. He says nothing yet of the kingdom because some knowledge cannot be shared until its season.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Please tell me what Samuel said—an uncle's natural curiosity. Saul's silence on what matters most shows that he is learning discretion. Some words are treasures to be held until the time is right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He tells about the donkeys plainly, but concerning the kingdom, he says nothing. There is wisdom in knowing what to speak and what to keep close. The Lord's purpose reveals itself in its own time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mizpah—a place of covenant and remembrance, where Israel had gathered before. Here Samuel will call the people together, not for war, but to present the king Yahweh has chosen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel rehearses what God has done: Egypt, bondage, deliverance. Every king must know he rules under a Lord who has already proven His power and faithfulness. Saul's throne is built on that foundation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You have rejected your God, who saves you—a hard word, but true. When people cry for a king like the nations around them, they reject the simplicity of trusting the Lord alone. Samuel speaks plainly; he does not hide the cost of what they have asked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The tribe of Benjamin is chosen from all Israel—a narrowing down, a focusing of God's selection. From many tribes, one; from one tribe, soon one family; and from that family, one man.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the tribe, the Matrite family; from the family, Saul son of Kish. Yet when they call for him, he is not there—he hides among the baggage. The man God has chosen runs from his own calling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul hides, and Yahweh reveals where he is. No hiding place is deep enough to escape the Lord's purpose. Sometimes His will finds us in our fear, not in our boldness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Saul stood, he rose above the people from his shoulders upward—a figure set apart. The Lord chose a man whose outward strength matched the burden he would carry. Yet strength alone will not be enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel asks, Do you see him? and all the people shout, Long live the king! The kingdom is confirmed not in secret but before witnesses. What the Lord has chosen, the people now see and acclaim.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel wrote the regulations of the kingdom and laid them up before Yahweh—a written word, a record, a covenant. Even in Israel's new order, the book and the sanctuary remain the measure of all things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul went to his house at Gibeah, and the army—those whose hearts God had touched—went with him. He does not march with fanfare but gathers his own. Those who move with him know something has changed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Worthless fellows despise him and offer no gift; Saul holds his peace. Readers today hear an echo of what it costs to lead: some will doubt, some will mock, and a true king learns to say nothing in return. The vindication comes later, not in the moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
